text:
The recent discussions about the OPEC and non-OPEC production cuts and their impact on oil prices and U.S. shale oil production are a reminder that the upstream side of the oil industry (exploration and production of crude oil) tends to receive more attention than the downstream side of the business (the process of refining and the distribution of refined oil products). However, the refining industry is going through a lot of changes and faces significant challenges and/or opportunities in the coming years, depending on whom you talk to and which region of the world they operate in. While developing countries in Asia and the Middle East will continue to add distillation capacity in the coming years, mature markets such as the U.S. & Canada and Europe are likely to see only limited capacity additions over the long run. As regional demand shifts, we will see capacity growth in certain parts of the world combined with refinery closures in other parts. All these developments have an impact on the overall health of the refining industry and will change global trade flows in refined petroleum products.
In the developed world, there is little - if any - need for capacity expansion and the activity in the U.S., Europe and Japan is focused on improving efficiencies and maximizing the processing capabilities of existing facilities. Uncertainty about the future of oil prices encouraged a new wave of consolidation, restructuring and divestments in these countries. In 2016, both integrated oil companies and independent refiners have been involved in a number of transactions. Some of the more notable deals in the U.S. include the proposed purchase of Western Refining by Tesoro in November and the acquisition of ExxonMobil's 155,000 b/d Torrance refinery by PBF earlier this year. In March, Saudi Aramco and Shell agreed to separate the assets of their Motiva joint venture. Shell has also been shedding downstream assets in other parts of the world (Japan, Denmark and Australia for example) as part of a strategic realignment. The outlook for refining in 2017 is mixed. In most of the OECD countries, clean product inventories remain elevated. In Europe, both gasoline and distillate inventories are well above their 5-year averages, a result of high domestic refinery utilization and growing diesel imports from Russia, which is revamping its refining system. In the OECD Americas and OECD Asia, distillate stocks are also at the high end of their 5-year range. Global oil demand in the future is expected to be led by gasoline and Asia due to the continuing growth in the number of passenger cars in the region. U.S. product exports are expected to remain strong, in particular gasoline and diesel to Latin America. U.S. refiners benefit from a fall-off in Latin American refinery utilization, in particular in Mexico, Brazil and Venezuela.
In its recently published "World Oil Outlook", OPEC identifies four key trends that will impact the downstream industry. First, a slowdown in the pace of oil demand growth as a result of energy efficiency/conservation mandates which are driven by climate change initiatives. Secondly, demand continues to swing away from mature economies and toward developing Asia. Third, non-crude supplies, such as natural gas liquids (NGLs), gas-to-liquids, coal- to-liquids and biofuels, are expected to continue to grow, leading to a reduction in the proportion of new demand that will be satisfied by traditional refiners. The fourth and last trend identified by OPEC is the ongoing move towards higher quality products (i.e. fuels that meet low and ultra-low sulfur targets), like the recent adoption of the MARPOL Annex VI global sulphur cap mandate for marine fuels. This reinforces the long-term trend towards declining demand for residual fuels.
OPEC expects limited growth in product movements in the medium-term as some new refining capacity is projected to come online in demand centers, limiting requirements for imported barrels. However, in the long-term, product flows should recover in line with product demand growth.

In recent years, global oil markets have focused on the growth of the Strategic Petroleum Reserves (SPR) in China and - more recently - India as important drivers for crude oil imports and tanker demand. Relatively little attention has been given to the world's largest inventory of emergency crude oil, the U.S. SPR, stored in huge underground salt caverns along the coastline of the Gulf of Mexico. The U.S. SPR has a design capacity of 713.5 million barrels. The current inventory stands at approximately 695 million barrels, 266 million barrels of which is sweet crude, while the other 429 million barrels are sour crude. So far this year, there has been no movement in the SPR inventory, but this is likely to change in 2017. The Department of Energy recently announced that it will sell crude oil from the SPR as early as in January next year. The U.S. Congress has approved a number of sales and if all planned sales go ahead, the U.S. SPR could be reduced by some 190 million barrels between 2017 and 2025.
The idea of a national oil reserve traces its roots back to World War II, when Secretary of the Interior Harold Ickes advocated the stockpiling of emergency crude oil. Other efforts were made in 1952, 1956 (after the Suez crisis) and in 1970. However, it was the 1973-1974 oil embargo, when several Arab nations cut off oil flows to the United States, that triggered the establishment of the SPR. Exactly 41 years ago today, on December 22, 1975, President Ford signed the Energy Policy and Conservation Act, which mandated the establishment of an emergency reserve of up to one billion barrels of petroleum.
On July 21, 1977, the first oil - some 412,000 barrels of Saudi crude - was delivered to the SPR. The federal government accomplished the early fill of the SPR primarily through purchases on the open market and most of the oil for the reserve was acquired in the late 1970s and early 1980s. In 1994, President Clinton suspended direct purchases as a result of the federal budget deficit and in fiscal years 1996 and 1998, 28 million barrels were sold to reduce the deficit.
